title: Justice like water
hookLine: Amos the herdsman at Bethel: take away the noise of thy songs, and let justice roll down like waters (Amos 5:24)
tomorrow: a soldier met a freezing beggar at a city gate. what did he do?

lines: TAKE AWAY THE NOISE OF THY SONGS.
cards: The worship playlist, the lights, the best voices in town.

Then a herdsman from the village of Tekoa speaks at Bethel, where the king's sanctuary is, and says in God's name: "Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols."
The priest of Bethel tells him to go home and prophesy somewhere else.
Amos answers that he never trained for this: "I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit".

teach.h: THEY TURN ASIDE THE POOR IN THE GATE.
teach.b: Why silence the songs? The chapter is blunt, in God's voice: "I hate, I despise your feast days." Because the worship was loud and the courts were crooked.
Amos says the powerful "take a bribe, and they turn aside the poor in the gate from their right."

teach.h: LET JUDGMENT RUN DOWN AS WATERS.
teach.b: So the next line says what God wants instead: "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream."
Judgment there means justice, the fair hearing owed to the poor at the gate, and that's the word in today's line. Not a trickle on a feast day. A stream that doesn't stop.

teach.h: WORSHIP AND JUSTICE, NOT PULLED APART.
teach.b: That's Amos's teaching: worship and justice can't be pulled apart, and songs over crooked courts are noise.
Martin Luther King Jr. carried this verse into his own speeches.
And it lands small, too: justice is water, so it moves by steady flow, one fair act after another.

how: Jews read Amos among the prophets and Christians in the Old Testament; Amos 5:24 is often quoted by people working for fairness.

o: fairness that keeps flowing steadily, not just once
the calm feeling after you finally get even
a court ruling that ends a case in one dramatic day

games.q: the herdsman at Bethel: tap the pairs.
p: where the priest told Amos to go home
where the poor were turned aside

s: Amos was a trained prophet from a prophet's family
he said: I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son, but an herdman.
the King James Version says 'let justice roll down'
it says 'let judgment run down as waters'. the Hebrew word, mishpat, also means justice.
in Amos, God refuses to hear the music at Bethel
take thou away from me the noise of thy songs.

games.q: your choir throws a benefit concert, but the venue is shorting its cleaners' pay. what would Amos put first?
o: the cleaners' pay: justice flowing comes before the music.
the concert: beautiful worship pleases God whatever happens backstage.
neither: Amos only spoke to kings, not to ordinary choirs.
games.why: Amos: take away the noise of thy songs, but let judgment run down as waters.

practice: Think of one small unfairness within reach this week: someone talked over at work, a bill split wrong, a neighbor who can't get help. Decide one plain step that would set it a little more right.
Hold it in mind like water finding its way downhill.

wordCard.voice: Justice like water: fairness that keeps flowing, not a show on feast days. Amos's line, from a herdsman at Bethel.

orig.note: Hebrew: judgment, justice; the word the King James renders judgment in Amos 5:24.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: justice rolls down, a stream and not a song. Two weeks of living it, done.
